title: “LET HIM KISS ME WITH THE KISSES OF HIS MOUTH.” — YES, THAT IS IN YOUR BIBLE. BUT HAVE YOU EVER ASKED WHY GOD PUT IT THERE?
paragraphs: “LET HIM KISS ME WITH THE KISSES OF HIS MOUTH.” — YES, THAT IS IN YOUR BIBLE. BUT HAVE YOU EVER ASKED WHY GOD PUT IT THERE?

Before you blush, skip the verse, or turn it into something purely spiritual, understand this: God was never embarrassed by the love He created. And hidden within this ancient love poem is a truth about desire, intimacy, faithfulness, and the kind of love our wounded world is desperately trying to find.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine.” — Song of Solomon 1:2 (KJV)
Yes. You read that correctly.
Not from a romance novel.
Not from a forbidden manuscript.
Not from some scandalous love letter discovered beneath the ruins of an ancient palace.
From the Bible.
The same Bible that declares, “Be ye holy; for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16).
The same Bible that warns against sexual immorality.
The same Bible that tells us to flee youthful lusts.
And there, almost startlingly, in the middle of Holy Scripture, a woman speaks with breathtaking honesty about her desire to be kissed.
Not merely noticed.
Not admired from a distance.
Kissed.
And the Holy Spirit, who inspired Scripture, did not erase her words.
Think about that.
Somewhere along the way, many Christians became so uncomfortable discussing romantic desire that we began treating the subject as though holiness required pretending it did not exist.
We taught people how to avoid temptation, but sometimes forgot to teach them how to understand love.
We warned young people about lust without always explaining the beauty of faithful intimacy.
We spoke about marriage as a responsibility while rarely celebrating the affection God intended to flourish within it.
And when people encountered verses like Song of Songs 1:2, they sometimes laughed nervously, changed the subject, or hurried toward a spiritual interpretation that made the human romance disappear.
But what if we have been rushing past something beautiful?
What if the scandal is not that God allowed these words into Scripture?
What if the scandal is that we have sometimes been more embarrassed by God's good creation than God Himself?

Stay with me, because this ancient poem has something to say to the person who longs to be loved, the spouse who feels forgotten, the believer struggling with shame, and the wounded soul wondering whether love can ever feel safe again.
And to understand it, we must begin where the text begins.
With a woman who is not afraid to speak.
In the original Hebrew, Song of Songs 1:2 opens:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
The verb yishaqeni expresses the woman's wish that her beloved would kiss her.
The word neshiqot means “kisses.”
And pihu means “his mouth.”
There is no need to invent a secret meaning to make the sentence acceptable.
It is romantic language.
Personal language.
The language of longing.
The next Hebrew phrase is equally revealing:
כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Ki-tovim dodekha miyyayin.
Literally, “For your loves are better than wine.”
Here, dodekha refers to expressions of romantic love or affection. English translations commonly render the expression as “your love” or “your caresses.”
The Hebrew word yayin means wine, an image associated in biblical poetry with celebration, pleasure, and gladness.
She is saying that the affection of her beloved is more delightful than one of life's most celebrated pleasures.
Notice something remarkable.
The woman begins by speaking about her beloved in the third person: “Let him kiss me.”
Then she turns toward him directly: “For your love is better than wine.”
It is as though longing suddenly becomes an encounter.
The beloved is no longer merely someone she thinks about.
He is someone she addresses.
That is the intimacy of poetry.
And that is how the Song begins.
Not with an argument.
Not with a command.
Not with a theological lecture.
With desire.
But here is where careful reading matters.
The Song of Songs is ancient Hebrew love poetry. It celebrates the beauty of mutual affection, attraction, longing, delight, and committed love between a man and a woman.
Its language is sometimes tender, sometimes playful, sometimes intensely passionate.
And yes, sometimes startlingly physical.
That does not make it unholy.
It makes it a testimony to the goodness of embodied human love within God's created order.
Genesis tells us that God made humanity male and female and called His creation very good (Genesis 1:27, 31).
Before sin entered the world, Adam and Eve were naked and unashamed (Genesis 2:25).
Shame, exploitation, betrayal, and distorted desire belong to the tragedy of the Fall.
The human body itself is not the enemy.
Nor is faithful marital affection.
The enemy is sin, which takes what God made good and twists it away from His purposes.
And perhaps that is where this verse begins touching wounds we do not usually discuss in church.
Because not everyone reading these words has experienced love as something beautiful.
Some people hear the word kiss and remember tenderness.
Others remember betrayal.
Some remember their wedding day.
Others remember the person who promised forever and left.
Some know the comfort of being held by someone faithful.
Others know what it feels like to lie beside a spouse and still feel painfully alone.
And some carry memories they never asked for, where affection was used as a disguise for manipulation, coercion, or abuse.
If that is your story, please hear this.
What happened to you does not define your worth, and someone else's misuse of intimacy does not make you unclean.
God does not call exploitation love.
He does not call coercion romance.
He does not ask victims to pretend that betrayal was beautiful.
Biblical love cannot be separated from truth, faithfulness, dignity, and care.
The Song's celebration of mutual desire must never be twisted into permission to demand physical affection from another person.
Love does not erase another person's freedom or safety.
And the fact that Scripture celebrates romantic intimacy does not mean every believer must marry, experience sexual desire, or enter a romantic relationship to live a complete life.
Jesus Himself lived a fully holy human life without marrying.
The apostle Paul honored singleness as a genuine gift and calling (1 Corinthians 7:7–8).
Marriage is good.
Singleness can also be good.
Neither determines a person's value before God.
Our deepest worth is not established by whether another human being wants to kiss us.
It is established by the God who made us and, through Christ, calls us to Himself.
But we must not rush past the human beauty of the Song.
Because its poetry also confronts a painful misunderstanding that has wounded generations of believers.
Holiness is not the absence of affection.
And passion is not automatically the presence of sin.
The question is not merely whether desire exists.
The question is what desire loves, what it seeks, how it treats another person, and whether it submits to the wisdom and holiness of God.
A husband who cherishes his wife is not becoming less spiritual by expressing tenderness.
A wife who delights in her husband is not becoming less godly by expressing romantic affection.
Marriage was never intended to be merely two exhausted people sharing bills, responsibilities, and a roof while affection slowly disappears.
Scripture calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25).
That is not a command to dominate.
It is a call to sacrificial, self-giving love.
And the Song reminds us that marital love can include delight, admiration, pursuit, tenderness, and joy.
But there is another danger we must avoid.
We must not turn this poem into a promise that every relationship will feel like poetry every day.
Real love sometimes looks less like a passionate embrace and more like a tired husband washing dishes while his wife rests.
Sometimes it looks like an honest apology after a painful argument.
Sometimes it looks like staying beside someone through sickness.
Sometimes it looks like listening instead of defending yourself.
Sometimes it looks like rebuilding trust, slowly and truthfully, after damage has been done.
Romance can be beautiful.
But covenant faithfulness is not measured only by romantic intensity.
The love celebrated in Scripture is never meant to excuse selfishness simply because the emotions feel powerful.
And that brings us to a line later in the Song that deserves to be heard alongside its opening invitation.
“...love is strong as death...” — Song of Solomon 8:6 (KJV)
A few words later, the poet declares:
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it...” — Song of Solomon 8:7 (KJV)
The book that begins with a longing for kisses eventually speaks of a love so enduring that even overwhelming waters cannot extinguish it.
Do you see the movement?
Attraction matters.
Affection matters.
But enduring love must become more than a moment of desire.
It must have depth.
Faithfulness.
A strength that does not disappear when life becomes difficult.
And this is where the Song begins opening a window toward an even greater biblical story.
We need to be careful here.
Song of Songs 1:2 does not explicitly say that the kiss represents Jesus, salvation, the Holy Spirit, or a particular spiritual experience.
Its immediate meaning concerns the longing of a woman for her beloved.
We should honor that meaning rather than forcing every romantic image into a hidden Christian code.
Yet the Bible also uses marriage and bridegroom imagery to reveal the covenant relationship between God and His people.
The prophets speak of the Lord's covenant love for Israel (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19–20).
John the Baptist identifies Jesus as the bridegroom (John 3:29).
Paul uses marriage to illuminate the relationship between Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32).
And Revelation celebrates the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9).
These passages do not erase the human romance of Song of Songs.
They help Christians see that faithful human love belongs within a much larger biblical vision of covenant love.
A vision that reaches its greatest revelation in Jesus Christ.
And here, the story becomes personal.
Because some of us have spent years chasing the feeling of being wanted.
We wanted someone to choose us.
Someone to see us.
Someone to stay.
Someone to look at our scars and not turn away.
Maybe you tried to find that assurance in a relationship.
Maybe you kept forgiving promises that were never followed by change.
Maybe you confused being pursued with being cherished.
Maybe you accepted attention because you were starving for affection.
And maybe the hardest truth is that even after someone loved you, the emptiness remained.
Not because their love meant nothing.
But because no finite human being can carry the weight of being your savior.
No spouse can forgive your sins.
No romantic partner can conquer death.
No human kiss can reconcile you to God.
No relationship, however beautiful, can become the foundation of your eternal hope.
That place belongs to Jesus Christ alone.
And this is why the Gospel is not simply another love story.
It is the announcement that the holy God we have sinned against has acted in grace to save sinners through His Son.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Read those words again.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we made ourselves attractive to God.
Not after we finally overcame every temptation.
Not after our past became presentable.
Not after we learned to sound holy in public.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
The love of God in the Gospel is not sentimental approval of everything we do.
It is holy, costly, redeeming love.
Jesus did not come to tell us that sin does not matter.
He came because sin matters so profoundly that only His saving work could accomplish our reconciliation with God.
At the cross, divine justice and mercy are not treated as enemies.
Christ bears sin's judgment on behalf of His people, and forgiveness is offered through Him.
His resurrection declares that death does not have the final word.
And those who repent and believe in Him receive forgiveness and new life.
That is love beyond romantic poetry.
Not because romantic love is worthless.
But because the Gospel answers a deeper need.
The need to be reconciled to the God who created us.
Now think about another kiss recorded in Scripture.
Not the kiss of a lover.
The kiss of a betrayer.
In the garden of Gethsemane, Judas approached Jesus and identified Him with a kiss.
Luke 22:48 records Jesus asking:
“Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?”
What a terrible contrast.
In Song of Songs, a kiss expresses desired affection.
In Gethsemane, a kiss becomes the instrument of betrayal.
The same human gesture.
Two radically different meanings.
One associated with love.
The other with treachery.
And Jesus knew.
He knew who Judas was.
He knew what the kiss meant.
He knew the suffering that awaited Him.
Yet He continued toward the cross.
Not because betrayal was good.
Not because evil was harmless.
But because the Son of God had come to fulfill the Father's saving purpose.
And suddenly the distance between the beauty of Song of Songs and the agony of Gethsemane reveals something about our fallen world.
We were created for truthful love.
Yet sin has taught us to disguise betrayal as affection.
We were created for faithfulness.
Yet we have learned how easily promises can be broken.
We were created to love God and our neighbors.
Yet we have often loved ourselves at their expense.
And every one of us needs grace.
Not merely the person who betrayed us.
Not merely the person who hurt us.
Us.
We may not all have committed the same sins.
But all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23).
And none of us can rescue ourselves by pretending otherwise.
Perhaps you have never betrayed anyone with a kiss.
But have you ever said, “I love You, Lord,” while deliberately holding on to something He calls you to surrender?
Have you ever worshiped with your lips while your heart remained distant?
Have you ever wanted God's comfort while resisting His correction?
Have you ever asked Him to bless a relationship you knew was leading you away from obedience?
These are not questions meant to crush a wounded conscience.
They are invitations to honest repentance.
Because grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace brings sinners into the light.
And Jesus Christ is not afraid of what the light reveals.
Remember Peter.
He promised loyalty.
Then denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the shame.
The memory of his own words.
The realization that fear had exposed the weakness beneath his confidence.
But after the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Peter's failure was real.
His repentance mattered.
And Christ's mercy was greater than Peter's failure.
That is not cheap grace.
That is restoration.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to understand that distinction tonight.
You cannot undo every consequence of yesterday.
You cannot demand that every person you hurt trust you again.
You cannot erase another person's pain simply by saying you have changed.
But you can repent.
You can confess what is true.
You can turn from sin.
You can seek to make things right where possible.
You can receive the forgiveness offered through Jesus Christ.
And by His grace, you can begin walking in a different direction.
Your past may explain some of your scars, but it does not have the authority to write the final chapter of a life surrendered to Christ.
This is what we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing every earthly consequence.
But by forgiving sinners, making them new, and teaching them to live in the truth.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
What a promise.
Not a new image.
Not merely a better reputation.
A new creation in Christ.
And now return to that woman in Song of Songs.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
Her words remind us that human beings were made with the capacity to desire, to delight, to love, and to be loved.
But the Gospel reminds us that even our deepest human desires must find their rightful place beneath the lordship of Jesus.
Romantic affection is a gift.
It is not a god.
Marriage can reflect something beautiful about covenant faithfulness.
It cannot replace our covenant Lord.
A kiss can communicate tenderness.
It cannot save a soul.
And if you are single, widowed, divorced, abandoned, or grieving a love you thought would last, you are not excluded from the deepest hope of Scripture.
The invitation of Jesus is not reserved for people whose love lives are beautiful.
It is for the weary.
The repentant.
The brokenhearted.
The guilty who need forgiveness.
The lonely who need the presence of God.
The proud who need humbling.
The ashamed who need to know that forgiveness is possible.
Christ calls people to Himself.
And the love He gives is not fragile like human approval.
Romans 8:38–39 teaches that neither death nor life, nor any other created thing, can separate those who are in Christ Jesus from the love of God.
That is the assurance no romantic relationship can ultimately provide.
Maybe your marriage needs renewed tenderness.
Maybe your relationship needs honest boundaries.
Maybe your heart needs healing before you pursue another person.
Maybe you need to stop calling something love when it is destroying your obedience to God.
Maybe you need to ask forgiveness from someone you have hurt.
Or maybe you have been trying to earn God's love through religious performance, forgetting that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Wherever this finds you, do not merely admire the beauty of biblical love.
Allow Scripture to examine the condition of your own heart.
And if something has been exposed, do not hide it behind a religious smile.
Bring it to Jesus.
You can pray honestly:

“Lord Jesus, I have confused love with things that cannot save me. I have carried wounds, desires, fears, and sins that I cannot heal or overcome by my own strength. Forgive me. Teach me to love what is good, reject what is evil, and honor You with my heart, my body, and my relationships. Help me receive Your grace and walk in repentance and truth. Where I have been wounded, lead me toward healing. Where I have wounded others, teach me humility and responsibility. Make my life a testimony to Your redeeming love. Amen.”
And if this article uncovered something you have been afraid to admit, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
Not a performance of spirituality.
Not a competition over who sounds the holiest.
Just honesty before God.
You do not have to reveal private wounds publicly. Even a simple “Pray for me” is enough to invite your brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you.
And please, do not keep this message to yourself if someone you love needs to hear it.
Someone needs to discover what Scripture actually says.
Someone needs to know that biblical purity is not contempt for the body.
Someone needs to understand that desire requires wisdom, not denial of its existence.
Someone needs to hear that Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown distant from God, and even people who do not yet believe to follow along.
Because the goal is not simply to make people feel something for a moment.
It is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word and grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
And if Gospel Warrior has become a source of biblical encouragement in your life, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Not because giving money makes someone more saved, more holy, or more loved by Jesus.
That would be contrary to the Gospel of grace.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives shaped by love and obedience. Generosity can be one beautiful expression of that worship.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
But beyond any product or discount, our prayer is that you grow deeper in Christ.
If you are able and willing to help us continue and expand that work, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
Because ministry is not sustained by money alone.
It is sustained through God's grace and the faithful service of His people.
Some give.
Some write.
Some teach.
Some pray.
Some share.
And through ordinary acts of faithfulness, the truth of Christ continues reaching human hearts.
So before you leave, remember where we began.
A woman, thousands of years ago, expressing the beautiful longing to be kissed by the one she loves.
An ancient Hebrew poem that refuses to treat faithful human affection as something inherently dirty.
A Bible that celebrates love while calling us to holiness.
A Gospel that tells us human love, however beautiful, cannot save us.
And a Savior who entered our broken world, endured betrayal, carried our sins to the cross, and rose again so that all who trust in Him might have eternal life.
Perhaps the most important question is no longer whether the Bible really says, “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
It does.
The deeper question is whether we will allow the God who gave us the capacity to love to teach us what love is for.
Not worshiping desire.
Not despising it.
But bringing our whole lives under the gracious and holy lordship of Jesus Christ.
Because the most beautiful love story is not the one in which two imperfect people finally discover that they cannot live without each other.
It is the true story of the sinless Savior who gave Himself to redeem people who could never save themselves.
And that love does not merely make the heart race.
It calls the sinner to repentance.
It makes forgiveness possible.
It transforms the life.
It gives hope beyond the grave.
The kiss you longed for might have made you feel wanted for a moment, but the cross reveals a Savior whose redeeming love can change your eternity.
